reading.title: Pitching the Bike Rack
reading.purpose: Listen in as two students sharpen an argument for covered bicycle racks at their community center.
paras: Priya spread three index cards across the picnic table. "If we want to convince the neighborhood council to build covered bike racks, we need more than a wish," she told Devon. "We need a clear thesis, one sentence that states our main position right away."

Devon tapped his pencil. "How about this: covered racks at the center will keep bikes dry and encourage more families to ride instead of driving?" Priya nodded. "That works. Now let us test every claim we make so we can back it up with real numbers."

"I counted twenty-two bikes chained to the fence last Saturday," Devon said. "When it rained, everyone's seats got soaked. That feels like a valid point because it is based on facts we actually observed."

"Good," Priya replied. "Still, we should keep our request reasonable, meaning fair in cost and size. If we insist on a huge glass shelter, the council will say no. A simple metal awning fits the budget."

Devon smiled. "So our appeal should sound calm and practical, not angry. We want to advocate for riders publicly without making the council feel attacked. What makes a speech truly persuasive anyway?"

"Showing that the idea helps everyone," Priya said. "Fewer cars in the lot means less traffic near the crosswalk. At the end, we can urge the council to vote yes next month by handing out our map and cost sheet. Ready to practice from the top?"

choices: fair in cost and size rather than asking for too much
loud enough to grab the attention of the whole room
written down on three separate index cards before a meeting
already approved by the neighborhood council last month
qs.why: Priya defines reasonable right in the sentence as "fair in cost and size," contrasting a metal awning with an expensive glass shelter.

qs.q: Which sentence gives the real-world observation Devon plans to use as proof?
choices: Priya spread three index cards across the picnic table.
If we insist on a huge glass shelter, the council will say no.
"I counted twenty-two bikes chained to the fence last Saturday," Devon said.
Fewer cars in the lot means less traffic near the crosswalk.
qs.why: Counting twenty-two bikes chained to the fence is the firsthand evidence Devon observed.

ev.text: "I counted twenty-two bikes chained to the fence last Saturday," Devon said.

qs.q: Why does Priya mention less traffic near the crosswalk?
choices: She wants to complain about drivers who park near the picnic table.
She wants to show that even non-riders gain from covered bike racks.
She hopes the council will close the parking lot on Saturday mornings.
She thinks the crosswalk needs a new metal awning more than bikes do.
qs.why: Priya says a speech is persuasive when it shows the idea helps everyone, and less traffic benefits drivers and walkers too.

qs.q: What is this dialogue mostly about?
choices: Two friends argue over whether a metal awning or a glass roof looks better.
Two students decide to count how many cars park at the center on rainy days.
Two neighbors complain that the council never listens to young riders.
Two students plan a fair, fact-based pitch for covered bike racks.
qs.why: Priya and Devon organize their thesis, evidence, budget, and tone so their request to the council will be convincing.

clues.text: one sentence that states our main position right away
based on facts we actually observed

reading.retellFrame: To make their request convincing, Priya and Devon back up their ___ with ___ and keep the plan ___.
